title: The Utility at Three Mile Island Was Faking Its Safety Tests. The Fine Was $45,000.
title_candidates: The Utility at Three Mile Island Was Faking Its Safety Tests. The Fine Was $45,000.
The Company That Ran Three Mile Island Was Told Its Leak Test Measured Nothing. It Kept Using It.
The Utility at Three Mile Island Pleaded Guilty to Running a Meaningless Test. The Fine Was $45,000.
description:
At four in the morning a pump stops, and a valve opens exactly as designed. Thirteen seconds later it does not close. The light on the panel says it did.

At thirty-six seconds past four in the morning on the twenty-eighth of March, 1979, a feedwater pump tripped at the Three Mile Island Nuclear Station, Unit 2, near Middletown, Pennsylvania. Eight seconds in, the reactor scrammed. Control rods dropped into the core and the chain reaction stopped.

The relief valve should have closed at thirteen seconds, when the pressure came back down. It did not. The light on the control panel that told the operators about that valve was not wired to the valve. It reported the signal that had been sent to it. The signal said: close.

The valve stayed open for two hours and twenty-two minutes. In the first hundred minutes, some thirty-two thousand gallons escaped.

At fourteen seconds, an operator checked that the emergency feedwater pumps had started. He did not see two small lights showing that a valve on each emergency line was closed. One light was covered by a yellow maintenance tag. No one knows why the second light was missed.

During the first few minutes of the accident, more than one hundred alarms went off, and there was no system for suppressing the unimportant signals so that operators could concentrate on the significant alarms. The control room was not adequately designed with the management of an accident in mind. One of the men in that room put it plainly. I would have liked to have thrown away the alarm panel. It wasn't giving us any useful information.

Each was a product of his training, training that did not adequately prepare them to cope with the accident at TMI-2.

The technical specifications for Three Mile Island Unit 2 limited leakage to one gallon per minute from unidentified sources, and required an accurate and meaningful water inventory balance procedure to demonstrate that unidentified leakage was within allowable limits.

On the seventh of November, 1983, a federal grand jury in the Middle District of Pennsylvania returned an indictment against the company that ran the plant. Count 2 charged that the company was on notice that its procedure did not accurately and meaningfully measure the amount of unidentified reactor coolant leakage. Despite such notice, the defendant company continued to use such inaccurate and meaningless procedure in an effort to generate results which appeared to establish that reactor coolant leakage was within allowable limits.

The dates in that charge end on the morning of the accident. No document in this story says the faked tests caused the meltdown, and this film is not going to be the first to say it.

On the twenty-ninth of February, 1984, the company changed its plea. It pleaded guilty to one count, Count 2, the leak rate count, under the Atomic Energy Act and the quality assurance rules. It pleaded no contest to six others. And four counts were dismissed, among them Count 11, the only count brought under the ordinary federal criminal code. So the company was never convicted of lying to the regulator. It was convicted of running a meaningless test.

The total fine to be paid on all counts is forty-five thousand dollars. As a material condition of the plea agreement, the company also placed one million dollars in escrow for the Pennsylvania Emergency Management Agency, to assist in emergency preparedness and planning within twenty miles of the station. That million was not a fine.

On the Friday of the accident, the Governor of Pennsylvania advised pregnant women and preschool aged children to leave the area within five miles of the plant. Not a general evacuation.

Nobody died at Three Mile Island. On the basis of present scientific knowledge, the Commission wrote, the doses were so small that there will be no detectable additional cases of cancer, developmental abnormalities, or genetic ill-health. And it attached a caveat. The health effects of radiation dose levels of a few rems or less are not known.

As the evidence accumulated, it became clear that the fundamental problems are people-related problems and not equipment problems. The human beings who manage and operate the plants constitute an important safety system.

Whether or not operator error explains this particular case, given all the above deficiencies, we are convinced that an accident like Three Mile Island was eventually inevitable.

Prime Documentary makes long-form documentaries about ordinary people and the systems that fail around them. This episode is built from the 1983 federal indictment, the 1984 change-of-plea and sentencing transcript, and the report of the President's Commission on the Accident at Three Mile Island.

This film contains AI-assisted visualization: symbolic reconstruction, no real likenesses. Generated imagery is not evidence and is not presented as an authentic record.

TITLE: 83 chars, inside the 59-100 band; 'Three Mile Island' sits at character 15, inside the first 70; two sentences; opens on the institution; no colon, em dash, question mark, second person or all-caps word, and none of died/killed/deaths. First sentence is the title decision already settled in EP84_threemile_FACTS_LEDGER.v001.md section E (lines 93-113), which defends 'faking' from TM-203 ('continued to use such inaccurate and meaningless procedure in an effort to generate results which appeared to establish that reactor coolant leakage was within allowable limits', script.en.v001.md:204) and TM-314 ('it goes to the very heart of the leak rate test', :212); the film uses the word itself at :218 ('the faked tests'). Second sentence is script.en.v001.md:254 and :256 ('The total fine to be paid on all counts is forty-five thousand dollars' / 'Forty-five thousand dollars.'), and check_packaging_claims returns it SUPPORTED against both, plus :12. WHY THE LEDGER'S SECOND SENTENCE WAS NOT SHIPPED: the working title in section E is 'The Utility at Three Mile Island Was Faking Its Safety Tests. Then Came America's Worst Meltdown.' 'America's Worst Meltdown' is a superlative that appears in NO sentence of this episode's script, and 'Then Came' places the faking immediately before the accident, which is the exact implication episode_spec's forbidden_claims forbids ('That the falsified leak-rate tests caused the accident') and which the script refuses in terms at :218. The checker cannot see implication -- it says so in its own docstring -- so this was a human-side decision, and the ledger's own binding constraint (section E, closing paragraph) is what it was decided on. The fine is the substitute: it is a number, it is verbatim, and it carries the same shock. THUMBNAIL: the wording is declared under `thumbnail_text`, NOT `thumbnail_headline` -- measured 2026-08-27, 11 episodes used the latter and the claim checker never read one of them. 'IT BEGAN AT 4 A.M.' is the wording actually BURNED INTO thumbnail.threemile.01.v001.png, which was opened and read for this file. It comes back SUPPORTED on its outcome claim against script.en.v001.md:30/:96/:200, and the plant clock is script.en.v001.md:20 ('At four in the morning a pump stops') and :34 ('At thirty-six seconds past four in the morning on the twenty-eighth of March, 1979, a feedwater pump tripped'). Candidate 02 reads 'NO LIGHT.' over a frame in which a red tile is plainly LIT, so the words argue with the picture, and the phrase is in no sentence of the script. Candidate 03 reads 'STAY OR GO?' over cooling towers emitting a DARK PLUME -- episode_spec's era_setting says in terms that the towers emit water vapour and never smoke, and 'black smoke from a cooling tower' is in forbidden_subjects, so 03 is a factual error on its face and must not ship as it stands. That is a QC finding on the thumbnail set, not on this file. The `thumbnail` key holds a path and is skipped by the checker's path test, as intended. R3: nothing here says anyone died of the accident or was made ill -- the description carries the Commission's no-detectable-cases finding (TM-703) and, in the next sentence, the caveat that must travel with it (TM-704), exactly as episode_spec's forbidden_claims requires. Nothing here connects the leak-rate count to the meltdown: the description states that the charge ends on the morning of the accident and then refuses the causal claim in the film's own words (:216, :218). Nothing says the company was convicted under the false-statements law -- Count 11 is named as dismissed and as the only count under the ordinary federal criminal code (TM-205, TM-305). The $45,000 fine and the $1,000,000 to the Pennsylvania Emergency Management Agency are kept apart and the million is called not a fine (TM-304, TM-311). The advisory is described as an advisory to two named populations within five miles, not as a general evacuation (TM-709). The 3,300 person-rem figure and any reactor-order statistic appear nowhere (TM-702, TM-807). No individual is named, and the separate cheating case is not mentioned (TM-321). The company is not named anywhere in this package: the script calls it 'the company that ran the plant' and this file does the same.
